title: evening-latency-spiral-playbook-draft
content:
Purpose
This is a working playbook + incident review sketch for the evening latency spiral we saw on 2025-11-03 affecting Dedicated GPU pool 'dedicated-prod-eu-1'. Goal: capture signals, a short mitigation checklist suitable for on-call, and a set of follow-ups to reduce recurrence risk.

Background / summary
- Window: 2025-11-03 18:12-19:03 UTC (evening usage spike in EU region).
- Impact: 10–20% request error rate and p95 generation latency increased from ~220ms to 1.8s for 30 minutes across customers pinned to dedicated-prod-eu-1. No user data loss but client timeouts for a subset of API routes.
- Immediate customer-visible symptom: streaming responses stalled mid-token then resumed; some requests returned 502.
- Primary hypothesis (concurrent): a small set of long-running low-priority inference jobs caused KV cache churn + GPU memory fragmentation, triggering frequent GC/eviction cycles and autoscaler mis-evaluations.

Observed signals and quick evidence
- GPU utilization spiked to 96–99% on two nodes while others were ~60%. (Grafana panel: GPU Utilization by node).
- Per-node process list on node-7 showed two large inference containers with persistent sequence lengths >8k tokens and batch sizes of 48.
- Kernel crash logs: no driver OOM. CUDA memory allocation transient failures correlated with p95 spikes.
- Serving runtime logs: frequent 'KVCache.miss' log lines interleaved with 'batch_flush' events — indicates excessive context switching and cache thrash.
- Autoscaler decisions: controller scaled up then immediately down in a 3-minute flapping pattern. Autoscaler metrics show evaluation window=60s with CPU-based heuristics misclassifying GPU memory pressure as CPU idle.

Immediate mitigation executed (timeline)
- 18:18 UTC — oncall (Ethan) identified skewed per-node GPU usage and isolated node-7 by draining new sessions (kubectl cordon + scale down daemon).
- 18:22 UTC — manually evicted two suspected noisy containers (kubectl delete pod ...) after confirming via labels and job ids from task metadata. This reduced the GPU utilization on node-7.
- 18:26 UTC — temporary patch to autoscaler: raise evaluation_hold to 180s and ignore transient mem_pressure signals from nodes with >85% utilization for 120s. Patch deployed as a feature-flagged config in k8s configmap (rollbackable).
- 18:35 UTC — p95 latency trending back toward baseline; streaming issues mostly resolved by 18:45 UTC.

What worked
- Node-level isolation (cordon + eviction) reduced tail latency quickly.
- Having task metadata attached to pods (job-id, user-id, priority) allowed rapid identification of noisy jobs.
- Feature-flagged autoscaler config allowed a fast mitigation without a code rollback.

What did not work / gaps found
- Autoscaler heuristic coupling to CPU signals is brittle for GPU-heavy workloads. The evaluation window is too short for long-tail inference jobs, causing scale flapping.
- No quick 'soft-throttle' for noisy inference jobs: eviction is heavy-handed and caused customer retries.
- Monitoring lacked a clear 'kv-cache-thrashing' alert; we had to infer from combined KV miss logs and batch flush cadence.
- Runbook steps for long-sequence/long-batch detection were incomplete; oncall had to improvise shell commands.

Draft runbook (for oncall)
1) Triage basics
- Check global GPU pool health (Grafana: GPU pool overview). Look at p95 latency, request error rate, per-node gpu_util.
- Confirm if autoscaler is flipping scale decisions rapidly (see autoscaler-controller dashboard: decisions per minute).
- Check recent deploys (last 24h) via deployment dashboard and Slack #deploys for correlation.

2) If one/few nodes are hot (skewed utilization)
- Cordon the node: kubectl cordon <node-X> (prevents new pods scheduling).
- List pods by gpu-labeled namespace: kubectl get pods -o wide --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node-X>.
- Identify long-sequence or large-batch jobs by checking pod labels: job-seq-len, batch-size, user-priority. If labels missing, query task metadata service: curl -s "https://internal.metadata/job/<pod-name>".
- If noisy consumer and not higher-priority customer, evict gracefully: kubectl delete pod <pod> --grace-period=30 && annotate with reason=noisy-eviction.
- If unsure, cordon + drain new traffic only (prefer draining low-priority queues if supported).

3) If autoscaler is flapping
- Apply temporary hold: patch configmap redwood-autoscaler-config --type merge --patch '{"data":{"evaluation_window_s":"180","mem_ignore_threshold_s":"120"}}'
- Post in #sre-ops with patch id and rollback instructions.

4) If KV cache thrash suspected
- Search logs: rg "KVCache.miss|batch_flush" --json --glob 'serving-runtime*' | head -n 200.
- Increase kv-cache size for the pool via runtime feature flag (only for non-critical pools): PATCH /admin/pools/dedicated-prod-eu-1 {"kv_cache.max_entries": 200000}.
- If change not possible, isolate noisy pods as above.

5) Communication
- Open a Jira incident (REDINF-xxxx), set priority P2, list affected pools and customers.
- Post interim update every 20m to #incidents and #gcs-support with mitigation status and ETA.

Quick troubleshooting commands (notes to self)
- kubectl top pod --containers --namespace serving --sort-by=cpu | grep -E '(pod-name|job)'
- ssh node-7 "nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,memory.used --format=csv"
- curl -s https://internal.logging/query -d '{"q":"KVCache.miss service:serving-runtime | count() by pod"}' | jq .

Follow-ups and action items (owners and rough ETA)
- Short term (2w):
  - eng-sre: create a dedicated 'long-seq' detector alert (p95 seq_len > 4000 AND kv_miss_rate > X) (owner: Priya Kaur).
  - eng-serving-runtime: add a soft-throttle that reduces batch size for jobs with seq_len > 2k instead of immediate eviction (owner: Jian Li).
  - infra: change autoscaler default evaluation_window to 180s for gpu pools; add a mem-pressure dedup window (owner: Meera Patel).
- Medium term (6w):
  - product + solutions-eng: define customer SLAs and recommended max sequence sizes per dedicated tier. Add enforcement/guide in onboarding docs. (owner: Solutions Eng).
  - eng-serving-runtime: improve cache eviction algorithm to prefer small-eviction windows on nodes with high churn. (owner: research-ml lead).

Open questions / hypotheses to validate
- Were the noisy jobs user-initiated (customer) or internal test jobs that leaked into prod? Check job owner labels and billing account.
- Does increasing kv_cache size materially reduce p95 for long-seq jobs, or just hide the problem?
- Are there kernel-level memory fragmentation patterns we can surface earlier to preempt CUDA alloc failures?

Notes / raw snippets captured during the incident (verbatim)
- "node-7: pod/long-runner-tt12 seq_len=12048 batch=48 user=acct-6413"
- "autoscaler: scaleUp() decision window=60s memPressure=true cpuIdle=true -> scaleUp then scaleDown"
- "runtime: KVCache.miss x 234 in 30s; batch_flush cadence 3.2s (expected 0.8s)"

Post-incident quick log checklist for someone picking this up
- Pull node-level GPU profiles for 2025-11-03 17:50-19:30 UTC.
- Export serving-runtime logs for pool dedicated-prod-eu-1 for same window and run kv-miss aggregation.
- Verify autoscaler controller logs and configmap versions.

Appendix: quick links and refs
- Grafana pools overview: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/GPUPools/gpu-pool-overview
- Autoscaler README: confluence.redwood.ai/display/OPS/Autoscaler+Design
- Ticket created: https://jira.redwood.ai/browse/REDINF-4123

- Add synthetic test cases to stress dedicated pools weekly to catch flapping configs earlier (SRE + infra). (Meera)
- Schedule post-mortem meeting with serving-runtime and infra (invite list: eng-sre, serving-runtime, infra, solutions-eng).

-- end of draft --
